overview.title: 📖 Overview: Verses, Verdicts, and a Famous Cow
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 28a–28b
overview.hebrewSource: רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן, אַתָּה מוּמְחֶה לְבֵית דִּין, וְכׇל הַמּוּמְחֶה לְבֵית דִּין פָּטוּר מִלְּשַׁלֵּם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the derivation of the firstborn's two-day-one-night eating period with a final round of exchanges between Rav and the school of Rav, then tackles a genuine dilemma: does an owner get thirty extra days after a firstborn's first year only if the blemish appeared after the year, or also when it appeared during the year? A new mishna shifts to a slaughtered firstborn examined only after the fact, distinguishing eye blemishes (which can change after death) from body blemishes, and setting compensation for a non-expert's mistaken ruling. The daf's second mishna widens the lens to judicial error generally, exempting a recognized expert from having to pay for his mistakes — illustrated vividly by Rabbi Tarfon's famous misjudgment of a cow whose womb had been removed, and Rabbi Akiva's spirited defense of his colleague.

slides.title: 📜 Two More Rounds of Textual Sparring
slides.subtitle: Rav and the school of Rav mine the same verse for different halakhot
rows: 'יִהְיֶה לָּךְ' (it shall be yours) — stated twice
Teaches the firstborn is eaten two days and a night, like a peace offering — not just one day, like a thanks offering
Teaches that a BLEMISHED firstborn must also be given to the priest, a rule stated nowhere else explicitly in the Torah
Refers to the firstborn animals of all Israelites collectively
Refers to BOTH an unblemished and a blemished firstborn together

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: Each side must account for how the other reads the very same words — no phrase goes unexplained.

slides.title: ⏳ Thirty More Days — Extra, or Exclusive?
slides.subtitle: A genuine dilemma about the mishna's timing rules, tested and ultimately refuted

nodes.content: ❓ If a blemish appears within the firstborn's first year, does the owner get 12 months PLUS 30 more days — or are the two timeframes mutually exclusive?
🔍 A baraita: a blemish appearing on day 15 of the year lets the owner 'complete' 15 more days after the year ends — suggesting a 30-day total IS granted
❔ New sub-question: are those extra days counted from the END of the year, or from the DAY the blemish first appeared?
❌ Rabbi Elazar's claim — that the 30 days run from the moment the blemish appears — is directly refuted: the baraita only ever 'completes' days already owed, never grants a fresh 30

callout.label: Outcome:
callout.text: The Gemara explicitly declares this a תְּיוּבְתָּא — a conclusive refutation of Rabbi Elazar's position.

slides.title: 👁️ Cornea Blemishes vs. Body Blemishes
slides.subtitle: New mishna: examining a blemish only AFTER the firstborn has already been slaughtered

boxes.title: Cornea Blemishes (דּוּקִּין שֶׁבָּעַיִן)
items: Everyone agrees: forbidden if examined only after slaughter
Such blemishes can visibly change after death, making retroactive verification impossible

boxes.title: Body Blemishes — the Real Dispute
items: Rabbi Meir forbids: a decree, lest people confuse them with the unreliable cornea case
Rabbi Yehuda permits: no such decree is needed, since body blemishes do not change after death

boxes.title: Not All Corneas Are Equal
items: Some cornea blemishes change after death and some do not, as Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha demonstrated firsthand
This matters for evaluating witnesses who testify about a blemish's appearance before death

callout.label: Rabbi Meir's real motive:
callout.text: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak infers from the mishna's own wording that Rabbi Meir's ruling is a penalty for skipping the expert, not genuine doubt about the blemish itself.

slides.title: ⚖️ Payment for a Wrongly-Slaughtered Firstborn
slides.subtitle: When a non-expert's ruling leads to an improper slaughter
rows: The animal must be buried, and he pays the priest compensation from his own property
Payment for a small animal (sheep or goat)
A large animal represents a proportionally greater loss, justifying the higher share
Small-livestock owners already face a rabbinic decree restricting where they may graze their flocks, sparing the priest some effort — hence only a quarter-share is owed

callout.label: Why not pay the full loss?
callout.text: The Gemara treats these fractions as fixed rabbinic amounts, not a strict accounting of actual damages.

slides.title: 🐄 Rabbi Tarfon's Cow and the Expert's Exemption
slides.subtitle: New mishna: judicial error, illustrated by a famous incident

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: A cow's womb was removed. Rabbi Tarfon ruled it a tereifa; the owner fed it to dogs. The Sages of Yavne later ruled such an animal IS permitted.

lines.speaker: Todos
lines.text: The physician confirms: cows and pigs leaving Alexandria routinely have their wombs removed to prevent breeding elsewhere, yet live on normally.

lines.speaker: R' Tarfon
lines.text: 'Your donkey is gone, Tarfon!' — believing he must now sell his donkey to compensate the owner.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Rabbi Tarfon, you are an expert accepted by the court — and any such expert is exempt from paying for his errors!

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Why not simply say his ruling contradicted an explicit Mishna, making it automatically void — so the owner's loss was self-inflicted?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Rabbi Akiva gave two reasons: an error against an explicit Mishna is void regardless, AND even an error in judgment is covered by the court-expert exemption.

callout.label: Why give two reasons?
callout.text: The second reason extends protection even to errors of pure legal reasoning, not just clear-cut mishnaic mistakes — a broader principle worth stating on its own.

summary.principle: Precise textual derivations, precise timing rules, and precise categories of blemish or error all converge on protecting recognized expertise while holding non-experts accountable for the consequences of overstepping it.

flowSteps.content: 📜 Rav and his school complete their derivation of the firstborn's eating period and its gift to the priest, even when blemished
⏳ A dilemma about extra days beyond the first year is tested and ultimately refuted
👁️ Cornea blemishes are always unreliable after death; body blemishes are debated only due to a precautionary decree

columns.content: ⚖️ A non-expert's mistaken ruling costs him a fixed fraction of the animal's value
🐄 An expert accepted by the court is exempt from paying for his errors — as Rabbi Tarfon's cow illustrates

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Recognized expertise carries real protection from liability, but only within carefully bounded categories of error

quiz.q: According to the school of Rav, what does the doubled phrase 'it shall be yours' in Numbers 18:18 teach, beyond the connection to the two-day-one-night eating period?
o: That a blemished firstborn is exempt from all halakhot
That a blemished firstborn must also be given to the priest, a rule not stated explicitly elsewhere in the Torah
That only unblemished firstborns may ever be eaten
That the firstborn may only be eaten by the Kohen Gadol
quiz.e: The school of Rav reads the repeated phrase as teaching that even a blemished firstborn must be given to the priest — a halakha that otherwise has no explicit source anywhere in the Torah.

quiz.q: In the dilemma about extra days beyond the firstborn's first year, what does the baraita about a blemish appearing on day 15 ultimately prove, and what happens to Rabbi Elazar's specific claim?
o: It proves a full fresh 30 days is always granted, and Rabbi Elazar's claim is accepted
It proves only that existing days are 'completed' to a total of 30, and Rabbi Elazar's claim that the days run from when the blemish appeared is refuted
It proves nothing relevant to the question
It proves the owner never gets any extra time at all
quiz.e: The baraita shows that only a completion to a total of 30 days is granted, not a fresh 30-day grant from the blemish's appearance — directly refuting Rabbi Elazar's more generous reading, which the Gemara calls a תְּיוּבְתָּא.

quiz.q: Why does everyone agree that a cornea blemish examined only after the firstborn's slaughter renders it forbidden, regardless of the Rabbi Meir/Rabbi Yehuda dispute?
o: Because cornea blemishes are never valid grounds for slaughter
Because such blemishes can visibly change after death, making it impossible to verify retroactively whether they existed as claimed while the animal was alive
Because the Torah explicitly forbids all eye blemishes
Because Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda never discuss cornea blemishes
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that cornea blemishes are uniquely unreliable after death since their appearance can change, so no one can be certain after the fact whether the blemish was genuine and permanent while the animal lived.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna bar Manoaḥ, why does a non-expert pay only one-quarter the value of a mistakenly-slaughtered small animal, but one-half for a large animal?
o: Because small animals are worth more than large ones
Because a rabbinic decree already restricts where small-livestock owners may graze their flocks, sparing the priest some effort and justifying the lower payment
Because large animals are never subject to this payment rule
Because the difference reflects the animal's age, not its size
quiz.e: Rav Huna bar Manoaḥ explains that the decree restricting small-livestock grazing already spares the priest some burden regarding such animals, which is factored into requiring only a quarter-share payment rather than the half-share required for larger animals.

quiz.q: What two separate reasons does Rabbi Akiva give for why Rabbi Tarfon need not pay for the cow he mistakenly ruled a tereifa?
o: Both reasons concern only Rabbi Tarfon's wealth and status
An error contradicting an explicit Mishna is automatically void, and separately, an expert accepted by the court is exempt even for errors in judgment
Rabbi Akiva gives only one reason, not two
Both reasons rely solely on Todos the physician's testimony
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva offers two independent grounds: first, that an error against an explicit mishnaic ruling is automatically void; second, that even an error in legal reasoning is protected by the general exemption granted to an expert accepted by the court.
